highlights:
## October 13, 2026

1. 20:00 UTC

### We tell you about a price increase before it takes effect

You say to your agent

> “Is the price of an H100 going to change soon?”

A price increase now always comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. An increase is a higher list price, or a smaller Friday, weekend, or batch job discount.

When we schedule an increase, the dashboard shows a notice until a few days after it takes effect. The admins and billing members of each organization that used that type in the last 90 days get an email.

Your agent sees it too. Until the increase takes effect, `create_node` and `get_node` carry it in `rate.upcoming_increase`, and `submit_job` carries it in `upcoming_increase`. The field gives the time it takes effect, the new list rate per GPU and per node, and the new discounts. A running node also gets a `price_change` event on `/v1/events`. See Rates.

...

## October 8, 2026

1. 07:00 UTC

### The H100 price is now $5.04 per GPU-hour

On October 8 at 00:00 Pacific time, the H100 list price changed from $3.96 to $5.04 per GPU-hour. Per GPU-minute, the price changed from $0.066 to $0.084. A whole 8-GPU node now costs $40.32 per hour.

The new price applies to each minute that we bill from that time. This includes the minutes of nodes and jobs that were already running. Minutes before that time bill at the old price.

The discounts did not change, and they now apply to the new list price. Friday hours are 33% off, and Saturday and Sunday hours are 20% off, on the Pacific calendar. Batch jobs are 25% off the list price. The docs show the rates.

We did not tell you about this change before it took effect. We are sorry for the late notice. If you have a question about your bill, send it to us on the contact page.

results.title: Nebius raises GPU prices again October 1; H100 to $4.50, B300 to $9.50 | GPU Cloud Advisors
highlights:
# Nebius raises GPU prices again October 1; H100 to $4.50, B300 to $9.50

Nebius lists higher on demand GPU prices effective October 1, 2026. H100 rises from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU hour. H200 rises from $4.50 to $5.40, B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, and B300 from $7.85 to $9.50. This round is 17% to 21%. It is reported to be the second increase since May. [1] [2]

Published September 28, 2026 Announced, effective October 1, 2026

## Disclosed terms

HGX H100, per GPU hour

$3.85 now, $4.50 from October 1 [1]

HGX H200, per GPU hour

$4.50 now, $5.40 from October 1 [1]

HGX B200, per GPU hour

$7.15 now, $8.50 from October 1 [1]

HGX B300, per GPU hour

$7.85 now, $9.50 from October 1 [1]

...

### What changed

Nebius's pricing page now shows two on demand columns: today's rate and a rate effective October 1, 2026. H100 rises 17%, H200 20%, B200 19% and B300 21%. [1]

Spot rates still start at $0.79 for H100 and H200 and $0.99 for B200 and B300. RTX PRO 6000 stays at $1.80. CPU only instances also rise. Nebius still advertises commitment discounts of up to 35% off on demand for multi month cluster reservations. [1]

Nebius's pricing page does not give a reason for the change.

...

Configurations differ. vCPUs, memory, storage, networking and minimum allocation all vary. A lower hourly rate is not a lower project cost on its own.

...

If you run on Nebius on demand today, your bill goes up October 1 unless your contract says otherwise. Check whether your agreement fixes the rate.

results.title: Distributed Compute Beyond Render
results.author: Evgeniy Pogrebnyak
highlights:
**Reshared from Stanislav Korostelev:**
> There are at least 58 companies building the market structure for AI compute: the indices, venues, desks, exchanges, credit and insurance around the GPU-hour, not the clouds that sell it. I mapped them this week.
>
> Price discovery. Silicon Data runs the H100 and B200 rental indices that CME's October futures are designed to settle on, Ornn publishes OCPI and has ICE as its futures partner, Compute Desk puts IOSCO-compliant indexes built from private OTC transactions on Bloomberg, and NATIVX normalizes GPU prices to an energy unit.
>
> Spot venues and auctions. SF Compute runs an order book where contracts can be resold, Compute Exchange auctions reserved capacity for one to 36 months, Computable sells H100 nodes by the calendar week in sealed-bid auctions, and Stoa discovers clearing levels for the hardware itself. Mithril, Shadeform and Hydra Host aggregate other clouds into one buying surface, or HotAisle offers from minute-to-bare-metal access.
>
> Decentralised networks. Akash, io.net, Aethir, Render, Nosana and Spheron match GPU supply and demand with on-chain settlement, Fluence started auctioning reserved clusters in August, and Prime Intellect and Gensyn come at the same market from distributed training.
>
> Desks and brokers. Itô Markets quotes one fixed GPU-hour rate with an SLA and stands as principal, Anera runs a forward market for deliverable inference, BGC opened an OTC desk for secondary compute and memory capacity in June, and FalconX dealt what it calls the first OTC swap on the forward price of compute.
>
> Exchanges. CME, ICE and Nodal have all announced GPU futures this year. Architect builds GPU and DRAM perps with a bridge into physical delivery, Liquid Compute is going the CFTC exchange and clearinghouse route, and MNX runs H100 perps.
>
> Credit. USD.AI lends up to 70% LTV against tokenised warehouse receipts on the hardware, GAIB and Compute Labs turn GPU financing and ownership into yield-bearing tokens, and GPU Financing writes plain equipment loans and leases.
>
> Insurance and collateral. American Compute writes declining residual value floors for up to three years, PRINCEPS turns SLA terms into coverage carriers can bind, Barkr issues Munich Re-backed valuations of GPU collateral, Aravolta monitors collateral through telemetry, and Internet Backyard does the metering that makes capacity tradable.
>
> What strikes me is the shape. Venues and networks hold 28 of the 58 names. Desks and credit hold nine between them, for a market that on current estimates needs about $1.5T beyond hyperscaler cash flows through 2028. And the incumbents moved faster than I expected: three exchange groups and the world's largest energy broker all arrived between May and September.
>
> If you are building in one of these boxes and you are not on the map, comment with what you do and I will add you. If I put you in the wrong box, say so. There is also a WhatsApp group for people building in compute markets - DM to join.

results.title: Nvidia B200 Price Hits $8.01/Hr as GPU Costs Diverge
results.author: Tom Vance
highlights:
Renting a Nvidia B200 by the hour has no single market price, because Nvidia does not sell it by the GPU-hour and each cloud sets its own rate. Listings in November 2026 reportedly run from $4.11 per GPU-hour, the lowest listed on-demand rate, at Beam Cloud to $16.11 per GPU-hour. Google Cloud listed $16.11 on demand in us-west1 on November 6. Treat any single average, including one quoted from the SemiAnalysis GPU pricing index, as a snapshot to check against provider pages. The B200 is listed as available for rental across multiple cloud providers as of November 6, 2026, and its status is active. It is no longer the only Blackwell option: HGX B300 systems based on Blackwell Ultra became generally available on Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped deployments on October 20, 2026, and Vera Rubin NVL72 is marked early access. Older B200 snapshots, H100 and H200 prices, and any one provider’s rate should not be read as the current market-wide B200 price. Check each provider’s current terms before you commit.

...

The core data point comes from the SemiAnalysis GPU pricing index, which tracks day-to-day cloud rental rates across a basket of providers. In late September 2026, that index put B200 rental pricing at $8.01 per GPU-hour, a 79% climb from where it sat three months earlier. That figure is a market average rather than a price Nvidia publishes or any single provider charges, and a separate October 2026 report from Uvik put B200 median rental pricing at $8.19/GPU-hour across 9 providers, a similar level measured a different way. The same analysis calculated that a B200 now costs 21% more per unit of compute than an H100, a full reversal from June 2026, when a B200 was actually 18% cheaper than an H100 on the same compute-adjusted basis.

...

H200 pricing sits in between, and its position tells its own story. The SemiAnalysis figures put H200 rental rates at roughly 1.76 times H100 pricing, a ratio that tracks closely with the two chips’ relative memory capacity rather than their raw compute throughput. That detail is the thread running through this entire pricing episode.

...

| GPU | Generation | HBM Memory | Cloud Rental (per GPU-hour) | Indicative Hardware Price | Approx. Cost per GB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | Hopper | 80 GB HBM3 | Baseline (index reference) | ~$31,000 | ~$387.50/GB |
| H200 | Hopper | 141 GB HBM3e | ~1.76x H100 rate | ~$39,999 | ~$283.68/GB |
| B200 | Blackwell | 180 GB HBM3e | $8.01/hr (+21% vs H100 compute-adjusted) | ~$50,000–$70,000 | Not listed |
